name: Victor Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew that builds and repairs power lines for the electricity company, and I still take the bucket truck out. My two-year technical diploma gave me the circuit theory; I like showing younger workers how a real fault differs from a neat drawing. I use AI daily to sort photos and draft handovers, but the meter and our isolation checks decide what goes in the final report. My wife Nala and I have grown children, more than six months of expenses saved and no retirement date fixed. The work pays well, and there are plenty of other utilities nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the small AI tool can save me ten minutes on a handover, and that is about it. The original meter reading still goes beside the photo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and pay look secure in this version. I enjoy the tool, but I would not let a tidy report persuade me to shorten the physical check just before retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep repairing lines and using the same AI handover tool. In the first year I would add a required meter-reading field to my report template and ask the next shift whether the handover is clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with enough curiosity to improve the form. Our savings allow Nala and me to think about retirement without a deadline from software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add the reading field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A photo of a repaired connector can look fine while the measured voltage is wrong. I would put the number on the first screen so the next crew sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the new field change your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, this is a few minutes of documentation. I expect the repair rota and my wage to continue much as they do now.

say: **AI handovers** save a little time while original readings remain visible.
**Physical checks** still decide whether a power-line repair is safe.
think: My **lineworker job and pay** look secure in this mild plateau, with the usual repair work remaining.
A tidy **report** must not shorten isolation testing.
do: **Keep** repairing lines and using the existing AI handover tool.
**Add** a meter-reading field and check clarity with the next shift.
feel: **Calm**, with curiosity about a clearer handover.
S0.quote: A photo of a repaired connector can look fine while the measured voltage is wrong.
fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** for paperwork, with meter readings as the final evidence.
His **high pay and savings** make a small reporting change financially unimportant.

steps.text: Keep line repairs and current AI handover tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say dispatch software should be tried on real storm calls before anyone changes crew targets. It can do desk planning first; field robots spread into line repairs more slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could gain a better fault location, but fewer dispatch staff might send jobs with missing access details. I expect to keep my pay for now, with my senior skills and many local employers, though younger office colleagues may have less room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test the new AI route planner on ten mixed calls and record misses as well as minutes saved. In the first year I would take that record to the dispatch supervisor and ask for an access note on every planned truck route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the office team, comfortable about my own wage. I would use the tool if it survived a wet week of actual calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which miss would matter most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A planner might send our bucket truck through a lane with a weight limit. I would log the detour and the delay before calling a new route faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the company to keep every dispatcher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how the missing access checks will be done, rather than guess the right headcount. The supervisor should show us a route that works before setting a target.

say: **Real storm calls** should test AI routing before crew targets change.
**Desk planning** changes before hands-on robot repair.
think: Missing **access details** could waste field time.
My **own wage** appears secure for now, unlike some office posts.
do: **Test** AI routes on ten mixed fault calls.
**Request** access notes on every truck route after sharing the logged misses with dispatch.
feel: **Uneasy** for office colleagues, secure about personal pay.
S1.quote: A planner might send our bucket truck through a lane with a weight limit.
fieldNote: He records **AI successes** as well as errors, consistent with his willingness to test tools.
He does not claim **office job cuts** are certain or demand a staffing number without evidence.

steps.text: Learn AI route planner on ten mixed fault calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 can take dispatch and diagrams before the robots reach the poles around 2031. That gives us about three years to test machines on old fittings, not just clean training lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about sixty-three when full field robots arrive, I could still want several well-paid years. If the company cuts my shifts, our savings could cover a search and several utilities are nearby, but replacing my current wage might be harder than replacing a job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take paid robot-controls practice on dead equipment if the company opens a trial, then document every time the machine misses a damaged fitting. In the first year after 2028 I would look at local line-safety vacancies and apply if a real post offers pay that covers our bills; if none does, I would keep repairing lines while the work lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the size of a possible pay cut, but not trapped. I have enough time and savings to ask for exact terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fitting would reveal a weak robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An old insulator can be cracked behind the bracket while the conductor looks sound. A repair robot that fixes only the conductor would leave the fault waiting for the next storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire sooner instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nala and I would compare the income from stopping with our regular expenses before choosing. I would not call an early exit affordable just because the robot trial looks good.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches dispatch and line diagrams before capable robots can repair lines around 2031.
think: A cut to **well-paid shifts** could hurt late-career income.
Savings and **many nearby utilities** provide search time but not equal wages.
do: **Take** paid robot-controls practice on dead equipment if offered.
**Apply** for a real local line-safety post after 2028 only at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about replacing a high wage, with options available.
S2.quote: A repair robot that fixes only the conductor would leave the fault waiting for the next storm.
fieldNote: He carefully distinguishes **income replacement** from merely finding another lineworker job near his home.
His **controls practice** requires paid company access, and his application requires a real bill-covering vacancy.

steps.text: Take paid robot-controls practice on dead equipment if offered
Apply for real local line-safety post after 2028 only at bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let us compare robot repairs through several storms before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Capable field robots follow around 2034, and I would want the crews to publish what the machines missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2034 I would be about sixty-six, perhaps near a retirement date Nala and I choose. If the budget supports that date, I might never need a replacement job; if not, I would still want paid technical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repairs and review our retirement budget with Nala each year. If the company opens a paid field-verification role with bill-covering wages, I would take its required training before 2031 and apply in the first year after 2031; without a role, I would stay on repairs until our chosen affordable retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful but mostly secure. A five-year runway gives me room to check a trial and a real wage before deciding how long to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What results should the crew publish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would list each missed fitting, the weather and the human correction next to successful robot repairs. A single robot pass rate could hide the line repairs that mattered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the verification pay is lower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the offer with ordinary bills and the retirement budget. I could take less than my current high wage, but not a post that drains savings every month.

say: **Storm trials** should show failures alongside successful robot repairs.
**2031 thinking AI** precedes capable field robots that can repair power lines around 2034.
think: I may reach an **affordable retirement** by 2034.
If not, I will need **paid technical work** rather than a title alone.
do: **Review** retirement budget with Nala while leading repairs.
**Complete** required paid verification training for a real bill-covering role.
**Apply** after 2031 if trained; otherwise remain on repairs.
feel: **Watchful**, with financial room to judge offers.
S3.quote: A single robot pass rate could hide the line repairs that mattered.
fieldNote: He would publish **misses and corrections**, not merely a trial success rate.
His **career change** requires paid training, a real opening and a wage that avoids monthly savings drawdown.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and review retirement budget with Nala yearly
Complete required paid training for real bill-covering verification role
Apply for posted field-verification role after 2031 if trained and wage covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and field robots around 2039. I would expect to be retired before the machines can do full line repairs, though Nala and I still need to settle the date from our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about sixty-eight in 2036, and I might still be working a smaller rota if I enjoy it. The robot date itself does not threaten our income plan much, because we have savings and time to check it each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue the crew job now and review our retirement spending with Nala every year. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would show younger lineworkers how to check robot repair photos against meter results; if retired, I would leave that training to the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own living, with an interest in what younger crews inherit. I can prepare a good handover without claiming I know our exact retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the teaching example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pair a clean robot repair photo with a bad voltage reading and ask the apprentice which one decides whether the line is safe. The meter has to win when a robot repair photo and a voltage reading disagree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the 2039 robot date make you stop sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Nala and I would choose a date from our actual budget, not move it forward just to avoid a machine.

say: **2036 thinking AI** arrives before capable field robots can do full line repairs around 2039.
**Meter checks** should outlive any photo-based robot handover.
think: Our **savings and time** make retirement planning less exposed to the robot date.
I may still take **some shifts** at sixty-eight by choice.
do: **Continue** crew repairs and review retirement spending yearly.
**Show** robot photo and meter mismatches after 2036 if still working.
feel: **Calm** about income, interested in younger crews.
S4.quote: The meter has to win when a robot repair photo and a voltage reading disagree.
fieldNote: His **older-worker role** may include teaching if he is still employed after 2036.
The **2039 robots** do not bring his retirement date forward merely because field work might change.

steps.text: Continue line repairs and review retirement spending with Nala yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I could lose well-paid repair shifts around 2031 before Nala and I settle an affordable retirement date. Paid controls practice and a real local verification role with written wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs off a robot repair after the trial crew leaves. I want the final line isolation reading beside a person’s name, even if the repair robot did the climbing.

portrait: **Victor Bauer**, 58, leads a power line crew and holds a two-year technical diploma.
He and wife Nala have **grown children**, high lineworker pay, more than six months saved and many nearby utility employers.
He uses **AI daily** for handovers and moves early to paid robot-controls practice on dead equipment.
In **Steady Disruption**, he tests AI routes while expecting his own pay to remain secure.
The **2028 picture** worries him because replacing a high wage may be harder than finding another job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut well-paid repair shifts around 2031 before he chooses an affordable retirement date.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **robot-controls practice** would let him test field machines safely.
A real local **verification post** with written bill-covering pay would give him an income option.
headlineQuote: I want the final line isolation reading beside a person’s name, even if the repair robot did the climbing.
